title: US Congressman Says Israeli Settlers and Soldiers Detained Him
content: The US congressman Ro Khanna says he was detained during a recent visit to the occupied West Bank. Khanna, a Democrat from California, had travelled to the area to see conditions there for himself. According to his account, armed Israeli settlers stopped his vehicle first and refused to let his group pass. Israeli soldiers then arrived at the scene, but Khanna says they did not help his group leave. Instead, he says the soldiers appeared to be on friendly terms with the settlers. The incident took place near the Palestinian village of Khirbet Zanuta, in the hills of the southern West Bank. That part of the West Bank has seen repeated tension between settlers and local Palestinians. His group was only released after calls were made to the US embassy in Jerusalem. Since returning, Khanna has accused the Israeli military of lying about what happened. He argues that his own experience shows the daily reality that Palestinians face under occupation. If a US lawmaker can be held in this way, he says, ordinary residents have even less protection. The Israel Defense Forces gave a very different account of the events. The military said its troops dispersed the civilians and reopened the blocked road. It also insisted that its soldiers did not take part in blocking the road. So the two sides now disagree sharply about the basic facts of the case. Because the accounts are so different, it is difficult to say exactly what took place. Khanna has faced criticism from pro-Israel figures since he described the incident publicly. Some of his critics have questioned his motives for speaking out so openly. The story has drawn wide attention because it involves a sitting member of the US Congress. It has also renewed debate in Washington about settler violence in the West Bank.

title: A US Lawmaker's West Bank Detention Turns Into a Public Dispute Over the Facts
content: A trip meant to observe conditions on the ground has instead placed a US congressman at the centre of a public argument with the Israeli military. Ro Khanna, a Democrat from California, says he was detained during a recent visit to the occupied West Bank. By his account, armed Israeli settlers stopped his vehicle first and refused to allow his group to continue. Israeli soldiers arrived a short time later, but Khanna says they did nothing to help his group leave. The confrontation happened near the Palestinian village of Khirbet Zanuta, in the hills of the southern West Bank. It is an area that has seen repeated tension between Israeli settlers and the Palestinians who live nearby. His group was released only after calls were placed to the US embassy in Jerusalem. Reports of exactly how long the hold lasted vary, with accounts ranging from roughly an hour and a half to somewhat longer. Since returning, Khanna has publicly accused the Israeli military of lying about the episode. He has framed his own experience as a small window onto the far harder reality that Palestinians face under occupation. His point, in effect, is that if a US lawmaker can be held in this way, ordinary residents have even less protection. The Israel Defense Forces have offered a markedly different version of events. The military said its troops were sent to the scene, dispersed the civilians, and reopened the blocked road. It also stated plainly that its soldiers did not take part in blocking the road at all. That denial sits directly against Khanna's claim that the soldiers stood by while settlers held his group. As a result, the two sides now disagree not only about intent but about the basic sequence of what took place. The dispute has also drawn in pro-Israel figures, some of whom have criticised Khanna since he spoke out. A few have suggested that the timing of his account was designed to serve his own political interests. Khanna and his allies reject that reading and insist he simply described what he witnessed. For his supporters, the case is evidence of how settler violence can go unchecked in parts of the West Bank. For his critics, it is a political episode that Khanna has chosen to amplify for his own reasons. What gives the story unusual weight is that it involves a sitting member of the US Congress rather than an anonymous traveller. Journalists were reporting in the same area, which has helped keep the incident in the public eye. That detail has pushed the incident into the wider debate in Washington over US policy toward Israel and the occupied territories. It arrives at a moment when many lawmakers are already divided over how closely the United States should stand by Israel. For now, with two flatly opposed accounts on the record, the full truth of the encounter remains contested.

title: Trump Ally Lindsey Graham Dies Suddenly at 71
content: Lindsey Graham, a long-serving Republican senator from South Carolina, has died at the age of 71. His office said he died after a brief and sudden illness. Preliminary findings from the medical examiner pointed to a heart-related cause of death. Graham had served in the US Senate since 2003, making him one of its most familiar figures. He was preparing to run for re-election in November of this year. For much of his career, Graham was known as a strong voice on foreign policy. He often took a hard line on countries such as Iran and Russia. Graham had once been a sharp critic of Donald Trump before the 2016 election. Over time, however, he became one of Trump's most loyal supporters in the Senate. That change made him an important figure in many of the biggest political fights of recent years. The day before his death, he had travelled to Ukraine and met President Zelenskyy. According to his staff, there was no sign that he felt unwell before he died. News of his death sent shockwaves through Congress and drew tributes from many leaders. Politicians from both parties, as well as foreign leaders, praised his long career. His passing also leaves an empty seat that must now be filled. Under state law, the governor of South Carolina, Henry McMaster, can appoint a temporary replacement. A special election process will then decide who represents the state in the longer term. Because Graham had already won his party's primary, that contest is now open again as well. For Republicans, a seat they expected to keep easily has suddenly become uncertain. For now, both parties in Washington are adjusting to the sudden loss of a well-known senator.

title: The Sudden Death of Lindsey Graham Reshapes a South Carolina Senate Seat
content: The death of Lindsey Graham has removed one of the most recognisable figures in the US Senate almost overnight. Graham, a Republican from South Carolina, has died at the age of 71, his office said. According to that statement, he died after a brief and sudden illness, with little public warning. The suddenness of the news caught even his own colleagues off guard, since he had been active in public life only days earlier. Preliminary findings from the District of Columbia medical examiner attributed his death to an aortic dissection linked to heart disease. Because those findings are described as preliminary, officials cautioned that the full picture could still change. Graham had served in the Senate since 2003, giving him more than two decades of influence in Washington. He was preparing to run for re-election in November when he died. Throughout his career he was best known as a foreign policy hawk, taking hard lines on Iran and Russia. He argued repeatedly for a strong American role abroad and for firm support of allies such as Ukraine. His political relationship with Donald Trump followed an unusual path over the years. Before the 2016 election he had been a sharp critic of Trump, but he later became one of his most loyal allies. That shift made him a central figure in some of the Trump era's most consequential battles in the Senate. Strikingly, Graham had travelled to Ukraine the day before his death and met President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. According to a senior aide, there had been no sign that he was feeling unwell before he died. News of his passing sent shockwaves through Congress and drew tributes from political leaders at home and abroad. Figures from both parties set aside their differences to acknowledge his long service and forceful style. His death also creates an immediate practical problem, because his Senate seat is now vacant. Under South Carolina law, Governor Henry McMaster is expected to appoint a temporary replacement to fill it. A special election process will then follow to choose who serves the remainder of the term. Because Graham had already won his party's primary, his death reopens the contest for the nomination as well. For Republicans, that turns a routine re-election into an unexpected fight over one of their safer seats. Candidates who had stood aside may now reconsider, and the state party faces some difficult early decisions. For the wider Senate, it means adjusting to the loss of a lawmaker who shaped debate for years. His absence will be felt in particular in discussions over foreign policy, where his voice carried real weight. The coming weeks are likely to bring both public mourning and quiet manoeuvring over the succession. For now, though, Washington is absorbing the sudden departure of a senator few expected to lose this soon.

title: After Weeks of Speculation, McConnell Reveals a Fall Put Him in Hospital
content: For weeks, Washington was full of questions about the health of Mitch McConnell, the veteran Republican senator from Kentucky. The 84-year-old had vanished from Congress, and his office had said very little, which only fueled the speculation. Reporters pressed for answers, colleagues traded rumours, and the silence itself became a story. On Sunday, McConnell finally broke that silence with a public statement. He revealed, for the first time, that a fall had led to his hospitalization. In addition to the injury from the fall, he had been treated for a case of mild pneumonia. According to his statement, doctors carried out a battery of tests to try to determine exactly what had caused him to fall. Such tests are often used to rule out more serious underlying problems in an older patient. The results, and what they mean for his long-term health, were not spelled out in full. McConnell said that he was now regaining his strength, but he was careful to add that he would not return to work quite yet. The wording suggested a recovery that is under way but not yet complete. It also left open the question of exactly when he might reappear in the Senate. He offered an unusually personal explanation for why he had stayed quiet for so long. People of his generation, he suggested, often hesitate to share the vulnerability that comes with growing older. That reluctance, in his telling, helped explain the weeks of silence that had left colleagues and reporters guessing. It was a rare moment of openness from a politician known for his tight control of what he says in public. McConnell is no ordinary member of the Senate. He has represented Kentucky since 2003 and spent years as one of the chamber's most powerful figures. For much of that time he shaped how his party voted and how the Senate ran its business. That long record is part of why so much attention followed his sudden disappearance. His absence, therefore, was felt keenly by his party at a time when every vote counts. With several senators away, the balance of power in the chamber can shift on any given day. His current term is set to end in early 2027, and for now his priority is clearly his recovery rather than his return. By putting out a detailed statement, McConnell appeared to be trying to calm the concern that his long absence had created. He signaled that he intends to finish his term rather than step away early. Even so, he stopped short of giving a firm date for his comeback to the Capitol. For now, both his party and the public will simply have to wait for further news of his progress.

title: Chip Boom Sends South Korea's Exports Soaring in Early July
content: South Korea's exports jumped 53.9 percent in the first 10 days of July compared with the same period a year earlier. The main reason for this strong result was a surge in semiconductor shipments. In those 10 days, the country's outbound shipments reached $29.8 billion. That was a big rise from the $19.3 billion recorded in the same period last year. According to the Korea Customs Service, this was the highest figure for any 10-day period it has ever recorded. The previous record stood at $28.6 billion, so the new number clearly passed it. Semiconductors were the star of the story. Chip exports nearly tripled to $11.2 billion, providing most of the momentum behind the increase. This shows how strong the world's hunger for advanced chips has become. Many of these chips are used in computers, phones, and artificial intelligence systems. Imports also went up, rising 17.4 percent to $23.5 billion. Even so, the country still enjoyed a trade surplus of $6.4 billion for the period. In other words, Korea still sold much more than it bought. Some of Korea's biggest markets showed sharp growth. Exports to China rose 88.7 percent to $7 billion, while exports to the United States climbed 43.2 percent to $4.91 billion. Growth to China was especially strong, almost doubling from a year earlier. title: A Split Week for Korea: Record Chip Listing, But the Market Turns Bearish
content: In July 2026, South Korea's stock market delivered two headlines that seemed to point in opposite directions within the space of a single week. On one hand, the benchmark Kospi index slid into a bear market, falling more than 20 percent from the record high it had reached in June. On the other, one of the country's biggest chipmakers pulled off the largest US listing ever completed by a foreign company. The decline was driven above all by a heavy selloff in the two firms that dominate the index, Samsung Electronics and SK hynix. Their shares dropped steeply over just a handful of trading sessions, and because the pair now account for roughly half of the entire market's value, their weakness dragged the whole index sharply lower. That share is striking when you consider that the two companies made up only about a quarter of the market at the end of the previous year. In effect, South Korea's stock market has become a concentrated bet on the artificial intelligence trade, which magnifies both its gains and its losses. Earlier in the year, that same concentration had helped make the market one of the best performers in the world, which is exactly why the reversal felt so sudden. The trigger for the selloff was growing doubt about how long the big technology companies would keep pouring money into AI. If that spending were to slow, demand for the memory chips these Korean firms supply could cool as well, and investors decided not to wait around for confirmation. Adding to the unease was a lack of clarity about how the chipmakers would enforce their long-term supply agreements with customers. What made the moment especially unusual was the timing: the chipmakers were still posting strong profits even as their share prices fell. That gap shows how stock markets often trade on expectations about the future rather than on results that have already been reported. Against this nervous backdrop came a very different piece of news. Only days earlier, SK hynix had raised 26.5 billion dollars by selling new shares in the United States, in a deal that beat the record Alibaba set with its debut back in 2014. The offering was heavily oversubscribed, a clear sign that many global investors still wanted a stake in the memory-chip business at almost any price. The two stories together capture the strange mood around the AI boom. There is genuine confidence in the earnings power of these companies, but there is also a fear that the whole rally has climbed too far, too fast. For a country whose fortunes are now so closely tied to a couple of chipmakers, that tension is likely to shape its markets for some time to come.

title: EU Warns Meta Over 'Addictive' Design on Facebook and Instagram
content: The European Commission has warned Meta that Facebook and Instagram may be breaking the European Union's digital rules. In preliminary findings published on July 10, 2026, the Commission said the two apps use an addictive design that pushes people into compulsive use. It pointed to several features, including infinite scroll, autoplay, push notifications, and highly personalized recommendation systems. According to the Commission, these features are built to keep users on the apps for as long as possible. For example, when a video ends, autoplay simply starts the next one, so it is easy to keep watching. Officials said they were especially concerned about the effect on minors and other vulnerable users. They also argued that Meta had not properly checked the risks these designs pose to people's physical and mental well-being. In particular, the Commission said Meta had ignored data on how much time teenagers spend on the apps at night. Meta does offer some tools to manage screen time, and some are switched on by default for teenagers. But the Commission said these tools can be dismissed too easily and do not really reduce how much time people spend. To fix the problems, the EU wants Meta to disable features such as autoplay and infinite scroll by default. It also wants the company to add effective screen-time breaks and to make its recommendation systems less focused on engagement. If the findings are confirmed, Meta could face a very large penalty. The fine could reach up to 6 percent of the company's total worldwide annual turnover. For a company as big as Meta, that would mean a bill of many billions of dollars. Meta rejected the findings, saying it disagreed with them. The company said the Commission had not taken proper account of the steps it has already taken to protect teens. Because the findings are only preliminary, Meta can reply before any final decision is made.

title: Brussels Puts Meta on Notice Over the 'Addictive' Design of Its Apps
content: The European Commission has accused Meta of breaking the European Union's digital rulebook, arguing that Facebook and Instagram are deliberately designed to keep users hooked. In preliminary findings issued on July 10, 2026, the Commission said the two platforms breach the Digital Services Act because their design encourages compulsive use. Regulators singled out a familiar set of features: infinite scroll, autoplay, push notifications, and the highly personalized recommendation systems that decide what appears in each user's feed. According to the Commission, these mechanisms are engineered to maximize the time people spend on the apps, rather than to serve their interests. The concern is sharpest when it comes to younger users, and the findings focus heavily on the effect of these designs on minors and other vulnerable groups. Regulators pointed in particular to evidence about how long teenagers stay on the platforms late into the night, and to the way short-video formats can pull them into hours of continuous viewing. Officials said Meta had failed to properly assess the risks that its choices pose to users' physical and mental well-being. The company does provide some screen-time tools, and certain ones are switched on by default for teenage accounts. But the Commission judged these safeguards to be largely cosmetic, noting that they can be dismissed too easily and do not lead to any meaningful reduction in usage. To bring the platforms into line, regulators want Meta to disable features such as autoplay and infinite scroll by default. They also want the company to introduce genuine screen-time breaks and to redesign its recommendation systems so that they are less driven by engagement. The potential penalty is substantial. If the preliminary findings are eventually confirmed, Meta could be fined up to 6 percent of its total worldwide annual turnover, a sum that would run into the billions of dollars. Beyond the money, the Commission can also order the company to change the way its products actually work. The case is significant because it goes beyond questions of content and targets the underlying architecture of the platforms themselves. In effect, Brussels is arguing that the very shape of these apps, and not just what appears on them, can cause harm. That is a notable shift, because for years the debate over social media focused mainly on harmful posts rather than on the design choices that keep people scrolling in the first place. Meta pushed back firmly against the decision. The company said it disagreed with the findings and that they failed to reflect the significant measures it had already taken to protect teenagers. Because the findings are only preliminary, Meta will now have a chance to respond before any final ruling is made. Even so, the case signals that European regulators are ready to challenge the business model that has made social media so profitable.

CASC is China's main state-owned space company. During the flight, the rocket delivered a satellite into its target orbit before the lower stage turned around and headed back. China took a different path entirely. A recovery ship waited out at sea with a net strung across a large frame on its deck. The market and the streets around it are usually crowded, especially in the evening and at weekends. According to officials, about 63 people were injured in the blaze, and many of them were in a serious condition. Witnesses described how the fire spread with alarming speed once it began. Thick, dark smoke quickly filled the crowded interior, making it difficult for people to see or breathe. In the confusion, many of those inside rushed toward the exits, desperate to escape the flames. Some people were separated from their friends as they searched for a way out. Video footage shared online captured a huge blaze raging through the building and smoke pouring from the entrance. The images gave a frightening sense of how fast the situation had turned deadly. Firefighters arrived at the scene and worked to bring the fire under control. It took them a considerable effort before the flames were finally put out. Rescue workers then carried the injured out of the building and rushed them to nearby hospitals. Medical staff have been treating the survivors, some of whom remain in a critical state. The pub is known as a lively venue in the northern part of the Thai capital, which made the loss of life especially shocking. For many regular customers, it was simply a familiar place to meet friends and relax. In the hours after the fire, the authorities launched an investigation into how the disaster unfolded. One of the central questions is what exactly caused the fire to start. Investigators are also examining whether the building had enough emergency exits for the number of people inside. Fire safety at busy nightlife venues has long been a concern in cities across the region. Overcrowding, blocked exits and flammable decorations can turn a small fire into a fatal disaster within minutes. In several past cases, poor safety standards have been blamed for high death tolls. For now, families across the country are waiting for news and mourning those they have lost. Community members have gathered near the site to share their grief and support one another. The government has promised a thorough review to prevent similar tragedies in the future. Such reviews often lead to stricter rules on capacity, exits and fire equipment in public venues. Owners may be required to install better alarms, clearer signs and wider exit doors. Whether those lessons are fully applied, however, will only become clear over time.

title: US Strikes Iran Again as the Strait of Hormuz Standoff Deepens
content: The United States has launched a new wave of strikes against Iran, sharply raising tensions in the Middle East. Washington said the strikes were designed to degrade Iran's ability to threaten shipping in the Strait of Hormuz. The strait is one of the world's most important waterways, and a large share of global oil is carried through it every day. It is a narrow channel that links the Gulf to the open sea, which makes it easy to disrupt but hard to replace. At the heart of the crisis is a direct dispute over who controls this narrow channel. The US insists that the strait remains open and that traffic is still flowing. Iran, on the other hand, has announced that it closed the waterway to shipping. President Trump has publicly declared the strait open to commercial traffic, despite Iran's earlier announcement of a closure. The two governments strongly disagree, and each side is telling a very different story about the situation at sea. For ordinary observers, it is hard to know which account is accurate at any given moment. Iran has also carried out wide-ranging attacks on US allies and military bases across the region. These strikes have widened the conflict well beyond the two main countries involved. The current escalation follows a ceasefire that the two sides reached in June. That agreement has been fraying badly, and both sides have exchanged strikes over several days. What began as a fragile pause now looks increasingly like a return to open confrontation. Analysts warn that the standoff could easily spiral into a broader and more dangerous conflict. A serious disruption in the Gulf would also threaten to push global energy prices higher. Because so much of the world's oil passes through the strait, even the fear of closure can unsettle markets. Shipping companies may reroute vessels or delay journeys until the risk becomes clearer. Higher shipping costs and insurance premiums could then be passed on to consumers around the world. Governments across the region and beyond are urging both sides to step back from further escalation. Several countries have offered to help mediate, hoping to revive the collapsing ceasefire. They fear that the longer the fighting continues, the harder it will be to stop. Oil-importing nations are especially anxious, since their economies depend on steady supplies from the Gulf. Some have already begun to review their reserves in case shipments are interrupted for a long period. For now, the competing claims about whether the strait is open or closed remain difficult to verify independently. Neither side has allowed neutral observers to confirm the true state of traffic through the channel. The coming days are likely to show whether diplomacy can slow the cycle of strikes and counter-strikes. Until then, the region remains on edge, and the risk of a wider war has not gone away.

Iran, on the other hand, has announced that it closed the waterway to shipping.
President Trump has publicly declared the strait open to commercial traffic, despite Iran's earlier announcement of a closure.
The two governments strongly disagree, and each side is telling a very different story about the situation at sea.
For ordinary observers, it is hard to know which account is accurate at any given moment.
Iran has also carried out wide-ranging attacks on US allies and military bases across the region.
These strikes have widened the conflict well beyond the two main countries involved.
The current escalation follows a ceasefire that the two sides reached in June.
That agreement has been fraying badly, and both sides have exchanged strikes over several days.
What began as a fragile pause now looks increasingly like a return to open confrontation.
Analysts warn that the standoff could easily spiral into a broader and more dangerous conflict.
A serious disruption in the Gulf would also threaten to push global energy prices higher.
Because so much of the world's oil passes through the strait, even the fear of closure can unsettle markets.
Shipping companies may reroute vessels or delay journeys until the risk becomes clearer.
Higher shipping costs and insurance premiums could then be passed on to consumers around the world.
Governments across the region and beyond are urging both sides to step back from further escalation.
Several countries have offered to help mediate, hoping to revive the collapsing ceasefire.
They fear that the longer the fighting continues, the harder it will be to stop.
Oil-importing nations are especially anxious, since their economies depend on steady supplies from the Gulf.
Some have already begun to review their reserves in case shipments are interrupted for a long period.
For now, the competing claims about whether the strait is open or closed remain difficult to verify independently.
Neither side has allowed neutral observers to confirm the true state of traffic through the channel.
The coming days are likely to show whether diplomacy can slow the cycle of strikes and counter-strikes.
Until then, the region remains on edge, and the risk of a wider war has not gone away.
